questions.question: What is recombinant DNA technology? List its main steps.
questions.solution:
Recombinant DNA technology is the construction of a new DNA molecule by joining DNA from two different sources and expressing it in a host organism.
Steps: (1) identify and isolate the desired gene from a donor; (2) cut the gene and a vector with the same restriction enzyme to give complementary sticky ends; (3) ligate the gene into the vector; (4) introduce the recombinant DNA into a competent host cell; (5) select and screen the cells that took it up; (6) multiply them through preferential multiplication and gene isolation; (7) grow the culture in a bioreactor; (8) extract and purify the product by downstream processing.

questions.question: What are restriction endonucleases? Explain their naming and the role of sticky ends.
questions.solution:
Restriction endonucleases are enzymes obtained from bacteria that recognise a specific palindromic sequence and cut DNA at or near it; bacteria make them as a defence against foreign DNA, protecting their own DNA by methylation. Each enzyme recognises one sequence, which is why they are called molecular scissors.
Naming uses the organism of origin: EcoRI comes from E. coli strain RY13, the fifth enzyme found; HindIII from Haemophilus influenzae serotype d.
Many cut a staggered cut, leaving short single-stranded overhangs — sticky ends — on both fragments. Because the same enzyme gives complementary overhangs on the gene and vector, the fragments can pair by base pairing and be sealed by DNA ligase.

questions.question: What is a cloning vector? Describe the features of pBR322 and explain insertional inactivation.
questions.solution:
A cloning vector is a small DNA molecule able to carry a foreign gene into a host and replicate there — plasmids, bacteriophages, cosmids, BACs or YACs.
pBR322 has an origin of replication that lets it multiply in E. coli, an ampicillin-resistance gene (bla) and a tetracycline-resistance gene as selectable markers, and several unique restriction sites including BamHI, PstI and EcoRI.
Insertional inactivation: because the restriction sites lie within a marker gene, inserting the foreign fragment destroys that gene. An insert at the BamHI site disrupts the tetracycline gene, so recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline — the failure to grow on tetracycline is what identifies them.

questions.question: Describe PCR and state why Taq polymerase is used.
questions.solution:
PCR (polymerase chain reaction) amplifies a specific DNA segment in vitro. Denaturation: the template is heated to about 94 °C so the strands separate. Annealing: two synthetic primers, complementary to the flanking sequences, bind each strand at a lower temperature. Extension: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides from the primers to copy the template. The thermal cycle is repeated, and each cycle doubles the copies, so a billion-fold amplification takes about 30 cycles.
Taq polymerase from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus is used because it survives the repeated high denaturation temperature, so fresh enzyme need not be added each cycle.

questions.question: How is DNA separated by gel electrophoresis? Why is DNA treated with a stain?
questions.solution:
DNA fragments, being negatively charged because of their phosphate groups, are loaded into wells of an agarose gel placed in buffer and subjected to an electric field. The fragments migrate towards the anode, and their speed depends on size: small fragments move faster through the gel pores than large ones, so the fragment mixture separates into bands according to length, which can be visualised under UV light and compared with a standard ladder.
Ethidium bromide or SYBR Green is added because DNA itself is colourless; the dye intercalates between bases and fluoresces under ultraviolet light, so the bands become visible and can be photographed and measured.

questions.question: Describe bioreactors and downstream processing in biotechnology.
questions.solution:
A bioreactor is a vessel in which the genetically modified organism is grown at controlled pH, temperature, oxygen and mixing so that the desired product accumulates — stirred-tank reactors with impellers, airlift and sparged reactors are common, in batch, fed-batch or continuous mode, with sterile conditions to prevent contamination.
Downstream processing follows: the cells are separated by filtration or centrifugation, the product is extracted and purified by chromatography or precipitation, and it is formulated, quality-tested and packaged. It is often the most expensive step, because the product must be separated from thousands of other molecules and must meet purity and safety standards, and it decides whether a product is commercially viable.
